note: General fishing tips for the Learn page (not rules). Size, bag and season are never kept here: they come from the rules data for the chosen state.

fish.name: Snook
fish.range: Florida's coasts (south of about Cedar Key and Cape Canaveral), south Texas, and the Caribbean.
fish.habits: Ambush feeders that hold beside current: mangrove edges, dock pilings, bridges, inlet mouths and beaches. They move into the inlets and onto the beaches in summer to spawn, and into warm canals and rivers when it turns cold.
fish.when: First light, dusk and night. Moving water matters most: an outgoing tide at an inlet or bridge is a classic setup.
baits: Live pilchards, pinfish, shrimp or mullet
White or olive swimbaits and jerk-baits
rigs: Free-line live bait on a fluorocarbon leader
Jig head with a soft swimbait
tips: Use a fluorocarbon leader of about 20–30 lb: snook have sharp gill plates that cut thin line.
Keep the bait close to cover, then keep the fish away from the pilings.
Hold it gently and let it recover in the water before letting go.
A fish that is too big or too small for the slot still has to go back.
fish.lookalikes: Fat snook and swordspine snook are smaller relatives. The lateral line running onto the tail is the snook's mark, and the lower jaw sticks out.
fish.release: Wet your hands, keep the fish in the water, support it under the belly and hold it facing the current until it swims off.

fish.name: Tarpon
fish.range: Atlantic and Gulf coasts from the Carolinas around to Texas, strongest in Florida.
fish.habits: Big silvery fish that roll at the surface to gulp air. They travel the beaches and inlets in late spring and summer and sit around bridges and channels at night.
fish.when: Night at lit bridges and inlets, and mornings along the beach. A moving tide helps.
rigs: Free-line live bait on a heavy fluorocarbon leader
Circle hook on a stout rod
tips: Use a circle hook and do not set the hook hard: let the line come tight.
When it jumps, bow to the fish (lower the rod tip) so the line does not snap.
Use strong gear and keep the fight short: a worn-out tarpon can die.
Never lift a big tarpon out of the water for a photo.
fish.lookalikes: Ladyfish are small and slender, and have no long last ray in the back fin. A tarpon's last dorsal ray is long and thread-like.
fish.release: Keep it in the water the whole time, revive it facing the current, and let it swim away strongly.

fish.name: Redfish (red drum)
fish.range: Atlantic and Gulf coasts from Virginia to Texas, most common from the Carolinas to Louisiana and Texas.
fish.habits: Bottom feeders over oyster bars, grass flats, marsh edges and mangroves. Small "slot" fish live inshore; big "bull" reds work the inlets and nearshore water.
fish.when: Rising tide at first light and dusk, on shallow flats. Look for tails sticking out of the water.
baits: Soft plastics on a jig head
rigs: Bottom rig with a circle hook and a light weight
Jig head with a paddle-tail bait
Free-line bait under a popping cork
tips: Fish the edges: oyster bars, mangrove roots and the drop-offs of flats.
Slow down with a spoon or jig and let it fall close to the bottom.
Cut bait works best when it is fresh and the scent drifts down current.
A black spot near the tail is common; more spots do not mean the fish is a different kind.
fish.lookalikes: Black drum have chin whiskers (barbels) and no tail spot. Redfish have one or more black spots near the tail.
fish.release: Big breeding fish are best released quickly, in the water, without lifting them by the jaw.

fish.name: Spotted seatrout
fish.range: Coastal waters from Virginia to Texas, thickest on the Gulf coast and in Florida.
fish.habits: Live on seagrass flats and sandy holes in bays. They move to deeper holes and channels when it is cold or very hot.
fish.when: Early morning and evening, and on moving tide over grass. Winter fish hold in deeper, darker basins.
baits: Live shrimp under a popping cork
rigs: Popping cork with a leader and a live shrimp
Jig head and soft plastic, twitched slowly
tips: Cast along the edges of the grass or over sand potholes.
A popping cork calls them in: pop it gently, then pause.
Use a light leader because trout can be line-shy.
Their mouths are soft: do not horse them in.
fish.lookalikes: Sand seatrout are paler and have few or no spots. Spotted seatrout have many round black spots, including on the tail.
fish.release: Wet your hands, hold the fish gently by the lower jaw or body, and ease it back.

fish.name: Flounder
fish.range: Atlantic and Gulf coasts, with different kinds in each region.
fish.habits: Flat ambush fish that lie camouflaged on sand and mud near inlets, docks, jetties and creek mouths. They move to the passes when the water cools.
fish.when: Moving tide near inlet mouths, especially an outgoing tide on cool days.
baits: Live finger mullet, mud minnows or shrimp
Soft plastic on a jig head, bounced on the bottom
rigs: Bottom rig with live bait
Jig head dragged slowly along the sand
tips: Fish slowly and feel for a gentle tap, then wait a moment before setting the hook.
Keep the bait on or very near the bottom.
Work the edges where sand meets structure.
Check the season and size rule before keeping any flounder.
fish.lookalikes: Several flounder species look alike; the state's rule usually covers all of them as one group.
fish.release: Handle it flat and wet, and slip it back belly down.

fish.name: Sheepshead
fish.range: Atlantic and Gulf coasts from Massachusetts to Texas.
fish.habits: Black-and-white striped fish with human-like teeth. They crowd around barnacle-covered structure: pilings, docks, jetties, bridges and rock piles.
fish.when: Winter and early spring are best, when they gather to spawn. Around slack tide with some movement.
rigs: Small, strong hook on a short leader, straight down beside the piling
tips: Fish tight to the structure: drop the bait right beside the piling.
Their bites are subtle: feel for the tap and set the hook firmly.
Use a small, sharp, strong hook (their teeth are tough).
Keep your line tight so they cannot dive into the barnacles.
fish.lookalikes: Black drum juveniles are also striped, but have chin whiskers. A sheepshead has big front teeth and no whiskers.
fish.release: Beware the spines in the fins: use a towel and pliers to handle.

fish.name: Black drum
fish.range: Atlantic and Gulf coasts from the northeast to Texas.
fish.habits: Bottom feeders around oyster bars, bridges, inlets and channels. Small ones ("puppy drum") live in the bays; big breeders go to the inlets and the surf.
fish.when: Cooler months, at night or in the early morning, on a moving tide.
rigs: Fish-finder or bottom rig with a circle hook
tips: Fish the bottom with enough weight to hold.
Be patient: they often pick at a bait before taking it.
Big ones can be tough fighters: use strong gear.
Large old fish are often wormy and tough to eat: smaller ones taste better.
fish.lookalikes: Redfish have a spot near the tail and no chin whiskers. Black drum have chin whiskers and no spot.
fish.release: Large breeders should be returned: they are the future of the fishery.

fish.name: Florida pompano
fish.range: Atlantic coast from Virginia to Florida and across the Gulf, thickest in Florida.
fish.habits: Silver, fast surf fish that run along beaches, sandbars and inlets, feeding on sand fleas and small crabs.
fish.when: Cooler months on the beach, on a rising or falling tide, at first light.
baits: Pompano jigs, often with a bit of shrimp
rigs: Pompano rig (two droppers with small hooks and bright beads) with a surf sinker
Pompano jig (a small bucktail), bounced along the bottom
tips: Cast just past the breaking waves and let the rig sit.
Sand fleas are the top bait: dig them where the waves wash back.
Keep the rig light: they are fast and bite quickly.
Check the size rule carefully: there is a minimum size.
fish.lookalikes: Permit are bigger and rounder. Palometa (and other jacks) look similar but have different shapes and fins.
fish.release: Handle with wet hands; they are delicate.

fish.name: Spanish mackerel
fish.range: Atlantic and Gulf coasts from the Northeast to Texas.
fish.habits: Fast schooling fish that chase small baitfish in open water near beaches, inlets and piers.
fish.when: Warm months, early morning and evening, where bait is being chased.
rigs: Small spoon on a short wire or heavy fluorocarbon leader
Live-bait free-line
tips: Watch for birds diving: that tells you where the bait is.
Use a short wire leader or heavy fluorocarbon: their teeth are sharp.
Retrieve spoons fast.
Eat them fresh: the meat is oily.
fish.lookalikes: King mackerel get much bigger and have a lateral line that dips sharply. Spanish mackerel have yellow-orange spots on the sides.
fish.release: Use pliers; teeth are sharp.

fish.name: Bluefish
fish.range: Atlantic coast from Maine to Florida, and parts of the Gulf.
fish.habits: Aggressive schooling fish that slash through bait near beaches, inlets and piers. Teeth are very sharp.
fish.when: Dawn and dusk, with moving water. They often show up in big schools.
rigs: Wire leader with a bait on a bottom rig
Metal lure cast and reeled fast
tips: Use a wire leader: otherwise you will lose lures.
Watch for splashing, birds and baitfish jumping.
Cut bait on the bottom works when they are around.
Bleed and ice them quickly if you plan to eat them: the meat is strong.
fish.lookalikes: Small bluefish can look like Spanish mackerel, but bluefish have a more robust body and a forked tail with no spots.
fish.release: Use long-nose pliers: never put fingers near the mouth.

fish.name: Mahi (dolphin)
fish.range: Warm offshore waters of the Atlantic, Gulf and Pacific.
fish.habits: Bright green-and-gold fish that hang around floating weed, debris and rips offshore. They are fast, acrobatic and travel in groups.
fish.when: Daytime offshore, around weed lines and floating objects.
rigs: Troll rigged ballyhoo or lures
Free-line a live bait near floating weed
tips: Find weed lines or floating debris.
When you hook one, others often follow: keep one in the water to hold the school.
They fight hard and jump: keep the line tight.
Eat them fresh.
fish.lookalikes: Bulls (males) have a tall squared head; cows (females) are smaller with a rounder head.
fish.release: Be careful with hooks; they thrash.

fish.name: Kingfish (king mackerel)
fish.range: Atlantic and Gulf coasts, mostly offshore and along piers in warm months.
fish.habits: Fast, toothy fish that chase bait near reefs, wrecks, piers and the edge of the beach.
fish.when: Warm months, early morning and evening.
baits: Live blue runners, pilchards or herring
rigs: Slow-trolled live bait with a stinger (second) hook and wire leader
Trolled lures
tips: Use a stinger rig: kings often cut the bait in half.
Use wire: their teeth are razor sharp.
Be ready for a fast, long run.
Handle with care.
fish.lookalikes: Spanish mackerel are smaller with spots; cero mackerel have a stripe.
fish.release: Use pliers and a gaff or net with care.

fish.name: Cobia
fish.range: Atlantic and Gulf coasts, mostly spring to fall.
fish.habits: Brown, powerful fish that follow rays, sharks and turtles, and sit around buoys, wrecks and channel markers.
fish.when: Spring migrations along the coast; sight-fish them from boats near the surface.
rigs: Heavy jig cast to a spotted fish
Live bait on a strong leader
tips: Keep a rod ready with a heavy jig: they appear suddenly.
Be careful bringing them aboard: they are strong.
Check size and bag rules closely.
They fight hard and may need a break before landing.
fish.lookalikes: Remoras look similar but have a sucker on top of the head.
fish.release: Handle with strong gear; revive before release.

fish.name: Red snapper
fish.range: Gulf of Mexico and the southeast Atlantic.
fish.habits: Bottom fish that live around reefs, wrecks, ledges and rock piles offshore.
fish.when: Daytime, over structure in deeper water.
rigs: Bottom rig with a circle hook and sinker
Knocker rig
tips: Seasons are short and strict: check before you go.
Use circle hooks and a descending device when releasing deep fish.
Fish the structure and keep the bait close to the bottom.
Report if rules require it.
fish.lookalikes: Vermilion and other red-colored snappers can look similar: know the difference.
fish.release: A descending device helps fish survive deep releases.

fish.name: Mangrove snapper
fish.range: Florida and the Gulf coast, Southeast Atlantic coast.
fish.habits: Smart, line-shy fish living around mangroves, docks, bridges and reefs; bigger fish offshore.
fish.when: Night at lit docks and bridges; around full moon.
rigs: Light leader and small hook with a live shrimp, free-lined
tips: Use light fluorocarbon leader and a small hook.
Chum helps draw them in.
They bite best at night.
Keep them away from pilings once hooked.
fish.lookalikes: Lane snapper and other small snappers look similar; check the rule for the right fish.
fish.release: Handle with wet hands.

fish.name: Yellowtail snapper
fish.range: Florida's Atlantic coast and the Keys, and the Caribbean.
fish.habits: Slender fish with a yellow stripe, found over reefs and wrecks, often rising in a chum slick.
fish.when: Daytime on reefs.
rigs: Light line and a small hook with chum, free-lined
tips: Chum and keep the bait drifting naturally.
Use light, clear line.
Be patient: they come up in the chum.
Check size rules.
fish.lookalikes: Other snappers have no bright yellow stripe and forked yellow tail like the yellowtail.
fish.release: Handle gently.

fish.name: Gag grouper
fish.range: Gulf and southeast Atlantic.
fish.habits: Bottom fish around ledges, reefs and wrecks; young ones live inshore near rocks.
fish.when: Cooler months for nearshore fish; daytime offshore.
rigs: Strong rod, heavy line, live bait just off the bottom
tips: Pull hard right after the bite so it does not reach the rocks.
Use strong gear.
Check season carefully.
Use a descending device for deep releases.
fish.lookalikes: Black, red and scamp groupers look alike; know the differences.
fish.release: Use a descending device.

fish.name: Greater amberjack
fish.range: Atlantic and Gulf, offshore.
fish.habits: Powerful fish that hold around wrecks, reefs and rigs.
fish.when: Daytime over structure.
rigs: Heavy jigs worked deep
Live bait on a strong rod
tips: Expect a hard fight.
Use stout gear and heavy line.
Check size rule.
Worms in the meat are common and harmless but unappealing.
fish.lookalikes: Almaco jack and banded rudderfish are similar but smaller.
fish.release: Quick release is best; they are tough.

fish.name: Striped bass
fish.range: Atlantic coast from Maine to the Carolinas, plus rivers, reservoirs and the Pacific coast.
fish.habits: Schooling fish that chase bait along beaches, rips, jetties and river mouths; also landlocked in many reservoirs.
fish.when: Dawn and dusk, with moving tide and bait around.
rigs: Live bait free-lined
Jig head with a paddle-tail
tips: Fish rips, points and jetties on moving tide.
Use a circle hook with live bait.
Slot or size rules vary: check closely.
Handle with wet hands.
fish.lookalikes: White bass and hybrid striped bass look alike; the state rule may treat them differently.
fish.release: Keep them wet and avoid holding by the gills.

fish.name: Largemouth bass
fish.range: Lakes, ponds and rivers across nearly all of the lower 48 states.
fish.habits: Ambush fish that hold near cover: weeds, lily pads, docks, fallen trees and drop-offs.
fish.when: Early morning and evening; in the heat go deeper or into shade.
rigs: Texas rig (worm with the point buried)
Carolina rig
Wacky rig
tips: Fish cover: weeds, docks, brush and edges.
Slow down in cold water and speed up when it is warm.
Set the hook firmly when you feel the weight.
Check for size and bag rules and special lake rules.
fish.lookalikes: Smallmouth and spotted bass look similar; the jaw on a largemouth goes past the eye.
fish.release: Hold the fish by the lower lip and support the belly; do not hang it by the jaw.

fish.name: Bluegill & panfish
fish.range: Lakes, ponds and slow rivers across the US.
fish.habits: Schooling fish that live near weeds, docks and shade, easy to catch and a good start for kids.
fish.when: Daytime, especially warm months; they nest in shallow water in late spring.
rigs: Small hook under a bobber
Tiny jig
tips: Keep the bobber small so they feel little resistance.
Fish close to the shore, docks and weeds.
Bring a pair of pliers: their spines can poke.
Check the bag limit.
fish.lookalikes: Many sunfish look alike: redear, green sunfish and others.
fish.release: Wet hands; handle gently.

fish.name: Black crappie
fish.range: Lakes, ponds and rivers across the US.
fish.habits: Schooling fish that gather near brush, docks and submerged trees.
fish.when: Spring (spawn) in shallow water; deeper in summer and winter. Often best at dawn and dusk.
rigs: Minnow under a bobber
Small jig fished slowly
tips: Find the brush and fish around it.
Use light line: they have thin lips that tear.
Slow, steady retrieves work best.
Check the length rule.
fish.lookalikes: White crappie have vertical bars; black crappie have scattered black spots.
fish.release: Handle gently; their mouths are delicate.

fish.name: Channel catfish
fish.range: Rivers, lakes and ponds across most of the US.
fish.habits: Bottom feeders that hunt by smell and taste, often along deep holes, channels and river bends.
fish.when: Evening and night.
rigs: Slip-sinker bottom rig with a circle hook
tips: Fish the bottom in deeper holes and current seams.
Let them take the bait for a moment.
Handle carefully: pectoral and dorsal spines can hurt.
Check state limits.
fish.lookalikes: Blue and flathead catfish are bigger; channel cats have a forked tail and spots when young.
fish.release: Hold the body behind the spines or use a lip-grip.

fish.name: Walleye
fish.range: Northern US lakes and rivers, the Great Lakes and the upper Midwest.
fish.habits: Fish with glassy eyes that feed at low light along drop-offs, rocky points and weed edges.
fish.when: Dawn, dusk and night.
rigs: Jig and minnow
Live-bait rig (slip sinker, leader, hook)
tips: Fish low light and cloudy conditions.
Keep the bait near the bottom.
Slow and steady works.
Season and size rules vary widely: check.
fish.lookalikes: Sauger are similar but have spots on the dorsal fin.
fish.release: Handle gently; watch the sharp teeth and spines.

fish.name: Rainbow trout
fish.range: Cold streams and lakes, mostly in the West, Great Lakes and mountains, and stocked widely.
fish.habits: Hold in cool, well-oxygenated water: riffles, pools, and the edges of current.
fish.when: Morning and evening; cold, clear water.
rigs: Small hook with split shot
Float with a small bait
tips: Use light line; trout can see well.
Work the edges of current.
Keep them cool and wet.
Check stocking schedules and rules.
fish.lookalikes: Brown, brook and cutthroat trout look different: check the spots and colors.
fish.release: Wet your hands; do not squeeze.
